Similar to the mobile refueling configuration, the hydrant and dispenser truck configuration would benefit from having clear regulations related to where refueling could occur and whether passengers could be on board while refueling. It is not yet clear how long the cryogenic dispensing process would take and thus how much additional time an LH aircraft would need to be grounded between flights (especially in the case 2 passenger loading cannot occur at the same time). As noted in Section 4.2.1.4, ZeroAvia’s liquid hydrogen mobile refueler is aiming for 40 kg of LH dispensed per minute (ZeroAvia 2025). 2 Other studies have noted refueling rates that achieve between 60 kg/min and 150 kg/min (Vertical Flight Society 2023; Stolwijk and Rooze 2025). For a regional turboprop, the storage tank size would be around 1,000 kg (see Table 11), meaning that the time for dispensing would be about 25 minutes with ZeroAvia’s dispensing rate. This estimate should be taken as an order- of-magnitude approximation. As LH technology matures and more information is available, 2 dispensing times will become more precise. In this paragraph, we discuss a few additional considerations for the three refueling configurations already discussed in this section (fixed refueling directly next to the bulk storage system, mobile refuelers, and liquid hydrogen distribution pipelines from the bulk storage to hydrant refueling points). First, safety zones should be developed while the aircraft is refueling in case of hydrogen spillage or ignition. In a configuration where refueling occurs directly next to the storage, this should be easier to comply with because the cryogenic storage tanks must be placed in a location with offset distances already considered. This might be harder to comply with if the desired refueling location is at the terminal gate. Hydrogen sensors should also be deployed at different points in the dispensing equipment to detect any leaks before, during, or after the refueling process. Before dispensing, aircraft fuel systems should be precooled to avoid excess boil-off gas and purged to avoid hydrogen mixing with oxygen. During the dispensing process, boil-off gas generation is inevitable, and procedures must be developed on what to do with the gaseous hydrogen in the onboard storage tank once the refueling process is complete. More exact specifications for each of these considerations are required before liquid hydrogen dispensing can become standard practice (Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025). The use of swappable LH storage tanks instead of refueling the aircraft would eliminate the 2 need for specific airport refueling procedures and equipment. Instead, this pathway would require guidance on how to go about loading and unloading tanks from the aircraft and an understanding of the logistics of transporting the modular tanks to and from the airport and aircraft.
